summary: Provides information on the Russian federal standard GOST R 34.10-2012 for digital signatures, for developers and users who need to generate and verify such signatures. It updates RFC 5832 and is informational.

eli5.summary: It describes a particular way to sign digital papers used in Russia.

questions: how does the gost digital signature work
subtitle: The Russian standard recipe for signing a message with elliptic curves and a GOST hash.

tldr.problem: Systems that exchange messages over insecure public channels need a way to prove who signed a message and that it was not altered. Russian certification rules call for the national signature standard, GOST R 34.10-2012.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is an English translation of the standard. It defines a signature scheme built on points of an elliptic curve over a prime field plus the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash, with one process to generate a signature and one to verify it.
tldr.outcome: It gives developers outside Russia a readable description of the algorithm, with test values for checking implementations. It is an Informational Independent Submission that updates RFC 5832.

today: RFC 7091 is an Informational Independent Submission that updates RFC 5832 and has not been obsoleted. The RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What GOST R 34.10-2012 Is
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2012 is the Russian federal standard for digital signatures. It was developed by the Center for Information Protection and Special Communications of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation, with the open joint-stock company InfoTeCS JSC. This RFC is an English translation of it.

The standard replaces GOST R 34.10-2001 from 1 January 2013. New systems presented for certification MUST use the 2012 standard and MAY also use the 2001 one for compatibility with existing systems. Use of the 2001 standard in current systems is allowed for at least five years.

It is meant for messages sent over insecure public telecommunication channels. Compared with the previous standard, it makes messages more resistant to forgery and loss of integrity. The RFC says the sister standard for hashing, GOST R 34.11-2012, is translated in RFC 6986, and the older signature standard in RFC 5832.
sections.eli5: A country updated its official way of signing digital papers, and this document explains the new way in English.

sections.title: Keys and Scheme Parameters
sections.content:
A signature scheme has three processes: generating a key pair, generating a signature and verifying it. GOST R 34.10-2012 does not define key-pair generation. The parties agree on it themselves. It does not define how to generate the scheme parameters either, and points to RFC 4357 for possible sets.

The security rests on the difficulty of computing a discrete logarithm in a group of elliptic curve points, and on the security of the hash function. The scheme has two size options. The prime q, the order of a cyclic subgroup of the curve, must satisfy either 2^254 < q < 2^256 or 2^508 < q < 2^512. The hash output length l is then 256 or 512 bits, and the signature is a binary vector of 512 or 1024 bits.

  • The signature key is an integer d with 0 < d < q.
  • The verification key is a curve point Q with d * P = Q, where P is a point of order q.
  • The curve is defined over a prime field, with coefficients a and b or an invariant J(E) that must not be 0 or 1728.

The RFC also requires that the curve order m is not equal to p, and that p^t is not congruent to 1 modulo q for t from 1 up to a bound B, which is 31 for the smaller size and 131 for the larger.
sections.eli5: Each person has a secret number and a matching public mark. Everyone agrees in advance on the rules of the maths playground, and there are a smaller and a bigger size to choose from.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying a Signature
sections.content:
Signing, called Algorithm I, takes the signature key d and the message M. It hashes the message to H, turns H into an integer and reduces it modulo q to get e (using 1 if e is 0). It then picks a random or pseudorandom integer k with 0 < k < q and computes the point C = k * P. The value r is the x-coordinate of C modulo q, and the process returns to choosing k if r is 0. Finally s = (r * d + k * e) mod q, again returning to choosing k if s is 0. The signature is the concatenation of the binary vectors for r and s.

Verifying, called Algorithm II, takes the signed message, the signature and the verification key Q. It checks that 0 < r < q and 0 < s < q, otherwise the signature is invalid. It recomputes e from the hash, computes v as the inverse of e modulo q, then z1 = s * v and z2 = -r * v modulo q. From the point C = z1 * P + z2 * Q it takes the x-coordinate R modulo q. If R equals r the signature is accepted, otherwise it is invalid.

A signed message is the message plus an appendix. The appendix holds the signature and may carry a text field, for example the signer's identifier or a time label.
sections.eli5: To sign, you mix your secret number with a fresh random number and the message's fingerprint. To check, anyone redoes the maths with your public mark. If the answers match, the signature is real.

sections.title: Test Examples
sections.content:
The last technical section is a reference appendix of the original standard, but it is not officially part of it. It lists example values for the parameters p, a, b, m, q and P, the signature key d and the verification key Q. They are recommended only for testing that an implementation of the algorithms is correct.

The numbers are given in decimal and hexadecimal. Numbers starting with 0x are hexadecimal, and a double backslash marks a number that continues on the next line. The appendix then walks through the signing and verification processes with these values.
sections.eli5: It is like an answer key at the back of a maths book, so you can check your own work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section consists of one sentence: this entire document is about security considerations. The security properties are those described in the standard itself, namely reliance on the discrete logarithm problem on an elliptic curve and on the strength of the hash function.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about keeping things safe, so it has nothing extra to add at the end.
